clue.text: Used a gas-mask

parts.note: wearing a gas-mask suggests protection, but all the wearer does through it is draw breath in and out

explanation.surface: Someone recalls putting on a gas-mask, perhaps in a wartime drill.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a military memory; the answer is simply what anyone in a mask does all the while, breathing.
explanation.definitionFit: Using a mask that filters air means having breathed through it, the plain physical sense of drawing breath.

clue.text: Embryo emblem of England

definitions.meaning: something at an undeveloped early stage
the red rose is England's national flower, here in its unopened form

explanation.surface: A tiny beginning of England's floral symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: An unopened flower is the undeveloped form of the bloom, and the red rose is England's national emblem.

clue.text: Hard case to discharge explosive demonstration

parts.note: a shell is the hard outer case of an egg or a nut
to fire a gun is to discharge it

explanation.surface: A tough character lets fly in an explosive display.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard case' reads as a tough person but is a hard outer case.
explanation.definitionFit: Bombardment by artillery is a noisy, explosive show of force.

clue.text: The devil leads the dean to strike

indicators.note: one piece leads, coming in front of the other in the answer

parts.note: an imp is a little devil
W. R. Inge, the 'Gloomy Dean' of St Paul's, was a famous columnist of the day

explanation.surface: A devil leads a churchman astray into violence.
explanation.walkthrough: Dean Inge of St Paul's Cathedral was widely known as 'the Gloomy Dean' in the 1920s and 30s.
explanation.definitionFit: To hit or encroach on something, as light hitting a surface, is the sense meant.

clue.text: Values seem set for a change

indicators.note: letters set out for a change are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A person's values seem settled, but they want something different.
explanation.definitionFit: To prize or regard something highly is to rate it, a verb sense of values.

clue.text: Well acquainted with the metric system?

definitions.meaning: skilled or knowledgeable in a subject
metre in poetry is its rhythm, so something set in metre is written in lines of poetry

explanation.surface: Someone is praised for knowing their way round metres and kilograms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Metric' here is poetic metre, not SI units: something put into metre has been turned into poetry.
explanation.definitionFit: Being knowledgeable about a subject is being practised in it; writing in metre is putting it into poetic lines.

clue.text: Room for T.V. ? It's a matter of opinion

definitions.meaning: a room for television is somewhere to watch, a spot for looking from
an outlook or way of seeing an issue

explanation.surface: A debate over whether to have a television room ends in differing opinions.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is literal: a place set aside for watching, a spot from which to look.
explanation.definitionFit: A position to watch from, and an opinion or stance on a question.

clue.text: Tracks for training

parts.note: training is read as running trains, not exercising: the rails they run on

explanation.surface: Athletes look for running tracks to train on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'training' looks like exercise, but it means running trains.
explanation.definitionFit: Rails laid for trains to run on are permanent tracks.

clue.text: Bind like that merciless beldame?

definitions.meaning: Keats's 'La Belle Dame sans Merci' has the knight in her thrall

explanation.surface: A spell is cast by a cruel old woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Keats's poem ends with the warning 'La Belle Dame sans Merci / Hath thee in thrall', so the merciless lady holds her victims captive.
explanation.definitionFit: To captivate or hold in thrall, as Keats's merciless lady does the knight.

clue.text: Race where one Sooty is left at the post

definitions.text: Race where one Sooty is left at the post

parts.words: Race where one Sooty is left at the post
parts.note: a horse race with a lottery attached, read as a stake left by a sooty chimney cleaner

explanation.surface: A horse named Sooty fails to leave the starting gate.
explanation.walkthrough: A sooty person is a chimney sweep, and a stake is a post; a race run for a lottery prize pool takes its name from both.
explanation.definitionFit: A lottery in which the pooled stakes go to whoever drew the winning horse is the classic race gamble.

clue.text: One gets no thanks for this small item

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I
O is a zero, nothing
ta is British informal for thank you

explanation.surface: A small gift brings its giver no gratitude.
explanation.walkthrough: TA is everyday British slang for 'thanks'. 'gets' and 'for this' only link the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek letter's name is used for a tiny amount, as in 'not one jot'.

clue.text: Political theory gives blow for peace an unusual form

indicators.note: giving words an unusual form means rearranging their letters into a new order

explanation.surface: A political idea twists a strike for peace into something strange.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual form' rearranges all of BLOW FOR PEACE AN, fourteen letters including the 'an'.
explanation.definitionFit: The doctrine that peace is kept when no single state or alliance outweighs the others is a theory of international politics.

clue.text: They need not keep to the left of course

definitions.text: They need not keep to the left of course

parts.words: They need not keep to the left of course
parts.note: road users in Britain keep left, but these are golf clubs, and a golf course has no rule of the road

explanation.surface: A remark on traffic: some motorists are excused the British keep-left rule.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' looks like 'naturally' but means 'on a golf course'; the long-hitting wooden clubs share their name with motorists.
explanation.definitionFit: A golfer's longest-hitting wooden clubs share their name with the people who steer cars.

clue.text: Renovate with a form of rush fibre

indicators.note: a different form of these letters means rearranging them

explanation.surface: Someone restores furniture using rush fibre for the seats.
explanation.definitionFit: To freshen up and restore is what a renovation does.

clue.text: Conveyance of a half crazy proposer

definitions.text: Conveyance of a half crazy proposer

parts.words: Conveyance of a half crazy proposer
parts.note: the music-hall song Daisy Bell has a suitor 'half crazy' with love, who offers a ride on a machine built for two

explanation.surface: A lovestruck suitor turns up in some odd vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: The song 'Daisy Bell' ends 'I'm half crazy, all for the love of you' and promises 'a ... made for two'; the proposer's vehicle is that tandem.
explanation.definitionFit: A two-wheeled pedal machine is a means of getting about, as in the tandem of the song.

clue.text: Reprimand giving players one way out

parts.note: the players in a play are its cast
the Roman numeral for one is I
a gate is an exit, a way out of a field

explanation.surface: A director scolds the actors, showing them the exit.
explanation.definitionFit: To scold or rebuke severely, a strong form of reprimand.

clue.text: Fish for Mistress Quickly, perhaps

definitions.meaning: Shakespeare's Mistress Quickly keeps the Boar's Head tavern, a woman who keeps a beer-house

explanation.surface: A fish dish is served to Shakespeare's tavern hostess.
explanation.walkthrough: Mistress Quickly is the hostess of the Boar's Head tavern in Shakespeare's Henry IV plays, a woman who sells beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: a herring-like fish, and a woman landlord of a tavern like the Boar's Head hostess.

clue.text: Maxi skirt for hill climbing ?

parts.note: a maxi skirt sits low on the legs, and the Austin Maxi was a car that needs its lowest ratio to climb hills

explanation.surface: A woman wonders whether a long skirt suits a hill walk.
explanation.walkthrough: A maxi skirt hangs down near the ankles, and the Austin Maxi was a British family car of the 1970s; both are low gear.
explanation.definitionFit: A car's lowest ratio gives power at slow speed, which is what climbing a steep hill needs.

clue.text: Painter with power over water

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits over the second, above it in the grid

parts.note: a watt is a unit of power
eau is French for water

explanation.surface: An artist paints a power station by the water.
explanation.walkthrough: Antoine Watteau was an 18th-century French painter of fêtes galantes.
explanation.definitionFit: Antoine Watteau was a French rococo artist known for scenes of fêtes galantes.

clue.text: Increases from one level to another

definitions.meaning: raises the amount or rate of something
climbs a stair to a higher level, literally

explanation.surface: Something goes up, rising stage by stage.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means raising a rate, and literally means climbing a stair to a higher level.

clue.text: The greenhorn is heard to require help

indicators.note: the word for a gullible person is said aloud and sounds like a word for aid

parts.note: a greenhorn is a naive person easily fooled, a sucker

explanation.surface: A novice needs assistance.
explanation.walkthrough: SUCKER, a dupe, sounds like the old word for aid.
explanation.definitionFit: Aid given in time of need, an old-fashioned word for assistance.

clue.text: "Not by —— windows only" (Clough)

parts.note: a line of Clough's poem 'Say not the struggle nought availeth' with the word before 'windows' left blank

explanation.surface: A line of Victorian poetry quoted with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Arthur Hugh Clough's poem ends 'And not by ___ windows only, / When daylight comes, comes in the light': the blank is the direction of sunrise.
explanation.definitionFit: The window that faces sunrise looks towards the dawn quarter of the sky, where daylight first comes.

clue.text: They may need hoarding

parts.note: hoarding reads as stockpiling, but in Britain a hoarding is a large board for advertisements

explanation.surface: Some things are best stockpiled away.
explanation.walkthrough: In British English a hoarding is a billboard, where advertisements are pasted up.
explanation.definitionFit: Printed advertisements and bills are displayed on large boards beside roads.

clue.text: Poisonous slippery creatures, not footwear for bathers

definitions.meaning: venomous snakes of the swamps of the southern United States
the name reads as soft leather shoes for the sea, which they are not

explanation.surface: A warning about venomous snakes, which are not swimming shoes.
explanation.walkthrough: The snake's name sounds like waterproof slippers, which the clue denies. The grid's spelling with one C and two Ss is an old variant.
explanation.definitionFit: The cottonmouth is a venomous pit viper of American swamps, whose name sounds like soft leather slippers for the water.

clue.text: Army Engineers adapt to water

indicators.note: to adapt something is to change it, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: REME is the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers, a British Army corps

explanation.surface: Military engineers adjust to working on water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Army Engineers' is not RE but REME, the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers; 'adapt' rearranges those four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A lake or pond is called by this old word, still found in English place names.

clue.text: Extravagant claim to be reasonable

parts.note: saying 'I am' is a claim to be something, shortened to I'M
moderate means reasonable, within sensible limits

explanation.surface: Someone extravagant insists they are perfectly sensible.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sits right beside the claim to the opposite: 'I'm moderate' run together makes a word meaning excessive.
explanation.definitionFit: Excessive, lacking restraint, is what an extravagant person is.

clue.text: Get ready for the spring

parts.note: spring is a leap, not the season: a cat bends low before it jumps

explanation.surface: Gardeners prepare for the coming season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the spring' looks like the season after winter, but it is a jump.
explanation.definitionFit: Bending low with limbs drawn in is how an animal prepares to leap.

clue.text: "It is well done, and fitting for a ——" (A. & C.)

definitions.text: It is well done, and fitting for a

parts.words: It is well done, and fitting for a
parts.note: Charmian's words over Cleopatra's body in Antony and Cleopatra, with the royal title left blank

explanation.surface: A line of Shakespeare quoted with its last word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: In Antony and Cleopatra, Charmian says over the dead queen 'It is well done, and fitting for a ___ / Descended of so many royal kings'; A. & C. names the play.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is a royal daughter's title, which Charmian gives Cleopatra as descendant of kings.
